title: Design the acre language
body: What an `.acre` file looks like: how it declares the canvas and the objects on it, and later how each object changes over time. Jack settles the syntax by writing files in a working version and reacting to them. Each version goes into `crates/acre/src/lang` and `scene` once it is small enough to try. Over those versions, pin down the top-level shape of a file, how time is written (seconds, frames, or both), and how a property is animated between two values.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ec73b0
notes.text: Settled so far, syntax still open: canvas coordinates are pixels with the origin top-left. Time is seconds in the model; the frame index belongs to the renderer. The domain is arrays, matrices, grids and simple plots, so text in cells and on axes is in the first version. First examples to design the syntax against: an array of numbers being sorted (highlight the compared pair, swap them) and a line plot that draws itself with points appearing.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ed765a
notes.text:
Jack wants joined editing in the acre GUI. The GUI holds a text editor beside the render. Editing the text re-renders the scene. Dragging or stretching an object in the render rewrites the source text. To support that, `lang` and `scene` need four things:

- a parser that keeps comments and whitespace, so acre can rewrite one literal and leave the rest of the file as typed
- the source span of every value in the scene
- an id on every scene object that carries through to the primitives it draws
- a way for `scene` to say which object is under a point on the canvas

A value computed from other values has no single literal to rewrite. A grid cell whose x comes from its index is one. The syntax design has to say what a drag does to such a value. Two options so far are to refuse the drag, or to rewrite the nearest literal that feeds it, such as the grid's origin. Neither is chosen.

Static images, diagrams and plots are the main use. Simple animations still matter.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/89ed765a
notes.text:
Jack can't judge a syntax on paper. He wants a language he can run and react to, with still images settled before animation. The syntax uses braces and should look nothing like Python.

v0 is the first version to play with. A file is a tree of nodes. A node is a kind, an optional name and a braced body of properties (`key values;`) and child nodes. The parser gives nothing a meaning. `scene` interprets each node kind, so a change of vocabulary leaves the parser alone. The node kinds in v0 are `canvas`, `box`, `ellipse`, `line`, `arrow` and `text`. v0 has no time.

Three earlier candidates are set aside until still images work. They were objects plus a timeline, inline keyframes on every property, and sequenced steps.
